posts.title: Salesforce — Zero to Hero
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

From complete beginner to job-ready

Salesforce runs sales, service, and marketing for a huge share of the world's companies, and the skills to configure it are in constant demand. This course assumes zero prior experience. You'll start by understanding what the platform actually is, why companies pick it, and how the ecosystem of admins, developers, consultants, and architects fits together. From there we get hands-on inside a free Developer org.

You'll learn to navigate Lightning Experience, work with objects, records, and fields, and understand how relationships tie your data together. We'll build your first report and dashboard so you can see business value immediately, then automate a real process with Flow without writing any code. By the end you'll have a working mental model of the platform and a clear map of where to specialise next.

Who it's for: career changers, students, business users, and anyone curious about a Salesforce career. What you'll leave with: a live Developer org, comfort navigating the app, your first automation, and a plan for the Admin, Developer, or Architect track. Every lesson is short, practical, and built on the same example org so the concepts compound.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Go from total beginner to job-ready Salesforce professional — the platform, admin basics, automation, and your first steps into development.

posts.title: What is Salesforce & the Ecosystem
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

What is Salesforce & the ecosystem

Salesforce is a cloud-based Customer Relationship Management (CRM) platform. At its core it stores the people and companies you do business with and the interactions you have with them, then layers sales, service, marketing, analytics, and app-building capabilities on top. Because it's delivered as software-as-a-service, there's nothing to install and upgrades arrive automatically three times a year in the Spring, Summer, and Winter releases.

The platform is a family of clouds. Sales Cloud manages leads, opportunities, and pipeline. Service Cloud handles cases and support. Marketing Cloud runs campaigns and journeys. Underneath them all sits the Platform itself, which lets you build custom objects, automation, and applications. Most of what you configure as an admin or developer works the same way across every cloud because they share the same data model and metadata engine.

Just as important is the ecosystem of people. Admins configure the org with clicks — fields, page layouts, automation, security. Developers extend it with code when clicks aren't enough. Consultants translate business needs into solutions, and Architects design how it all fits together at scale. Around them is a famously welcoming community — Trailblazers — with free training on Trailhead, local user groups, and a huge job market. AppExchange is the marketplace where partners sell ready-made apps that extend your org.

The takeaway for this course: Salesforce is both a product you use and a platform you build on. You don't need to memorise every cloud today. You need to understand that everything sits on one shared foundation, and that the skills you learn here transfer everywhere on the platform. In the next lessons we'll get you a real org and start clicking around.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: A plain-English tour of what Salesforce is, the products that make up the platform, and the roles in its ecosystem.

posts.title: Editions, Orgs & Signing Up for a Dev Org
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Editions, orgs & signing up for a Dev org

An org (short for organisation) is a single instance of Salesforce with its own users, data, and configuration. Every company that buys Salesforce gets its own org, fully isolated from everyone else's. When you build or learn, you work inside an org too. Understanding this boundary early prevents a lot of confusion: a change you make in one org never affects another.

Editions are the packaging tiers that decide which features and limits you get — Essentials, Professional, Enterprise, and Unlimited are the common paid ones, each unlocking more customisation, API access, and higher limits. For learning and building, the free Developer Edition is perfect. It's a full-featured org with small data and user limits, free forever, and ideal for experimentation.

To sign up, go to developer.salesforce.com/signup, fill in the form, and pick a unique username. A Salesforce username looks like an email address but does not have to be a real inbox — for example you@zerotohero.dev. Use a real email for the verification link, then set your password and security question. Within a minute you'll land in a fresh Lightning Experience org.

A few habits worth forming now. Bookmark your login page and note that Developer orgs live on login.salesforce.com. Keep your username and password in a password manager, because the username is permanent. If your org goes inactive for a long time it can be deactivated, so log in occasionally. Finally, remember that anything you break here is safe to break — that's exactly what a Developer org is for. With your org ready, the next lesson gets you comfortable moving around the interface.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Understand orgs and editions, then sign up for a free Developer Edition org you will use for the rest of the course.

posts.title: Navigating Lightning Experience
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Navigating Lightning Experience

Lightning Experience is the modern Salesforce user interface. When you log in you land on your home page. Along the top is the navigation bar with tabs for the objects in your current app, and on the far left the waffle icon opens the App Launcher — the menu of every app and item you can access. Apps are just curated sets of tabs; switching apps changes which tabs you see, not your data.

Click an object tab such as Accounts and you get a list view: a filtered, sortable table of records. List views are one of the most useful everyday tools — you can create your own, filter by any field, and switch between them from the dropdown at the top. Open a single record and you're on a record page, which is organised into the highlights panel, tabs or sections of fields, and related lists that show connected records like an account's contacts and opportunities.

The global search box at the top searches across objects at once — start typing a name and Salesforce returns matching records grouped by type. The gear icon in the top right opens Setup, where all configuration lives; keep that mental separation in mind: the app is where you do business, Setup is where you configure. The bell icon shows notifications, and your avatar controls personal settings.

Two shortcuts pay off immediately. First, favourite frequently used records and list views with the star icon so they're one click away. Second, learn the difference between editing a single field inline (click the pencil next to it) and opening the full edit modal. Spend a few minutes creating an account, adding a contact to it, and logging an activity. Once moving around feels natural, we can talk about what all this data actually is — objects, records, and fields — in the next lesson.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Find your way around Lightning Experience: the App Launcher, tabs, list views, record pages, and global search.

posts.title: Objects, Records, Fields & Relationships
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Objects, records, fields & relationships

Everything in Salesforce is data, and the data model is simpler than it first looks. An object is like a database table — Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case are all standard objects. A record is a single row in that table, such as one specific account named "Acme Corp". A field is a column, like the account's Phone or Industry. You can create your own custom objects and custom fields whenever the standard ones don't fit; custom items get a __c suffix in their API name.

Fields come in types that control what they store and how they behave: Text, Number, Currency, Date, Picklist (a fixed dropdown), Checkbox, Formula (a calculated read-only value), and more. Choosing the right type matters because it affects validation, reporting, and automation later. Every object also has a system Name field and a unique Id that Salesforce assigns automatically.

Relationships connect objects. A lookup is a loose link — a Contact looks up to an Account, but each can exist independently. A master-detail is a tight parent-child link where the child can't exist without the parent, inherits its sharing, and is deleted with it. A many-to-many relationship uses a junction object in the middle. These relationships are what let you navigate from an account to all its contacts and opportunities on the record page.

You can inspect any object in Setup under the Object Manager, where you'll see its fields, page layouts, and relationships. Try creating a custom object called "Project" with a lookup to Account, add a couple of fields, and create a record. That single exercise — object, fields, relationship, record — is the foundation everything else builds on. Next we'll turn this data into insight with reports and dashboards.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: The heart of the data model: objects as tables, records as rows, fields as columns, and the relationships that connect them.

posts.title: Reports & Dashboards Basics
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Reports & dashboards basics

Reports answer questions about your data, and dashboards put those answers on a single screen. A report starts from a report type, which defines the objects and fields available — for example "Opportunities" or "Accounts with Contacts". You then add columns, apply filters to narrow the rows, and choose a format. The four formats are Tabular (a simple list), Summary (grouped with subtotals), Matrix (grouped by rows and columns), and Joined (multiple blocks side by side).

Grouping is where reports become powerful. Group opportunities by Stage to see how many sit in each phase, or by Owner to compare reps. Add a summary field like Sum of Amount and you instantly have pipeline value per stage. Filters can be simple field filters, date ranges like "this quarter", or cross filters such as "accounts with at least one open case". Save the report into a folder so others with access can reuse it.

A dashboard is a collection of components, each backed by a source report. You choose a visualisation per component — bar, line, donut, gauge, metric, or table — and arrange them on a grid. Because every component points at a saved report, clicking through takes the viewer to the underlying rows. Dashboards refresh on demand or on a schedule, and a running user setting controls whose data permissions the dashboard respects.

A practical first build: create a Summary report of Opportunities grouped by Stage with Sum of Amount, save it, then create a dashboard with a bar chart component pointing at that report and a metric component showing total pipeline. That's a real, useful sales view in about ten minutes and it uses only clicks. Reporting is often where new admins deliver their first visible win. Next, we automate a process so the data keeps itself tidy.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Turn raw records into insight: report types, filters, groupings, chart types, and assembling a dashboard.

posts.title: Your First Automation with Flow
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Your first automation with Flow

Flow is Salesforce's primary automation tool. It lets you do things automatically that a user would otherwise do by hand: update fields, create records, send notifications, and call more advanced logic. Flow replaced the older Workflow Rules and Process Builder, so learning it today is time well spent. You build flows in the visual Flow Builder, dragging elements onto a canvas and connecting them.

The most common type is a record-triggered flow, which runs when a record is created or updated. You pick the object, the trigger condition, and whether it runs before or after the record is saved. "Before save" flows are fast and ideal for setting fields on the same record; "after save" flows can create related records or send messages. Inside the flow you use elements like Decision (branching logic), Assignment (set variable values), Get Records, Update Records, and Create Records.

Let's design a simple one in words: when an Opportunity is set to Closed Won, automatically create a follow-up Task for the owner to schedule onboarding. You'd use a record-triggered flow on Opportunity, a Decision element checking that Stage equals "Closed Won", and a Create Records element that builds a Task with the owner as the assignee. No code required, and it runs every time the condition is met.

A few best practices from day one. Give elements and variables clear names so the flow reads like a sentence. Add a fault path on elements that can fail. Test in your Developer org before anything real. And prefer one well-organised flow per object and trigger type rather than many overlapping ones, which keeps behaviour predictable. Flow is genuinely powerful — much of what used to require Apex is now click-built. In the final lesson we'll map out where you can specialise next.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Build your first no-code automation with Flow: triggers, elements, variables, and a simple record-triggered flow.

posts.title: Where to Go Next: Admin, Dev, Architect
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Where to go next: Admin, Dev, Architect

You now have a working org, can navigate the app, understand the data model, and have built a report and an automation. That's a real foundation. The next question is direction, and Salesforce offers several well-trodden paths that all build on what you've just learned.

The Admin path deepens configuration: security and sharing, advanced automation, data management, and change management. The entry certification is Salesforce Certified Administrator, followed by Advanced Administrator and platform-app-builder credentials. The Developer path adds code — Apex, Lightning Web Components, and integrations — starting with the Platform Developer I certification. Many people do Admin first and then Developer, because understanding the declarative platform makes you a far better developer.

Beyond those, Consultants specialise in a cloud such as Sales Cloud or Service Cloud and focus on translating business requirements into solutions, while Architects design large systems and pursue the demanding Application and System Architect tracks that lead to the prestigious Certified Technical Architect. There are also focused roles in Marketing Cloud, CPQ, Data Cloud, and analytics — several of which have their own courses on this site.

Your concrete next step: pick one path and commit to a first certification. If you're unsure, start with the Administrator credential — it's the broadest foundation and opens the most doors. Work through the matching Trailhead trailmix, keep practising in your Developer org, and build one small end-to-end project you can talk about in interviews. From here, the Apex Masterclass and LWC A–Z courses on this site are natural next stops for the developer track. You've gone from zero; the hero part is just consistent practice from here.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Map the Salesforce career paths — Admin, Developer, Architect and more — with certifications and a concrete next step.

posts.title: Apex Masterclass
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Server-side Salesforce, done properly

Apex is the strongly-typed, Java-like language that powers custom business logic on the Salesforce platform. This masterclass takes you from language fundamentals to production-grade patterns used on real enterprise teams. We treat Apex the way senior engineers do: bulk-safe by default, governor-aware, and covered by meaningful tests rather than assertions that only chase a percentage.

You'll master collections, write efficient SOQL and SOSL, and understand DML and the notoriously tricky save order of execution. We build triggers using a maintainable handler pattern, then bulkify everything so it survives a 200-record data load. The async chapters cover Future methods, Queueable, and Batch Apex with the trade-offs that decide which one to reach for. Finally we cover testing to 75%+ coverage the right way, with test data factories and assertions that actually verify behaviour.

Prerequisites: comfort with basic object-oriented programming and a Salesforce org. Outcome: you'll be able to design, write, and test Apex that scales, passes code review, and deploys cleanly. This is a paid, members-only course; the first lesson is free to preview.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

posts.title: SOQL & SOSL in Depth
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

SOQL & SOSL in depth

SOQL (Salesforce Object Query Language) retrieves records from a single object and its related objects. It looks like SQL but is tailored to the Salesforce data model — no arbitrary joins, but first-class relationship traversal instead. SOSL (Salesforce Object Search Language) is different: it performs full-text search across multiple objects at once, which SOQL cannot do.

// Child-to-parent traversal with dot notation
SELECT Id, Name, Account.Industry, Account.Owner.Name
FROM Contact
WHERE Account.Industry = 'Technology'

// Parent-to-child with a subquery
SELECT Id, Name,
       (SELECT Id, LastName FROM Contacts)
FROM Account
WHERE CreatedDate = THIS_YEAR

// Aggregate query
SELECT StageName, COUNT(Id) cnt, SUM(Amount) total
FROM Opportunity
GROUP BY StageName
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 100000

Relationship queries are the heart of SOQL. Traverse child to parent with dot notation up to five levels (Account.Owner.Name). Go parent to child with a subquery using the child relationship name (Contacts for the standard relationship, or your custom relationship name ending in __r). Filtering uses WHERE with the usual operators plus date literals like THIS_YEAR and LAST_N_DAYS:30. ORDER BY, LIMIT, and OFFSET control the result set.

Two bulk-safety rules dominate real code. First, never put SOQL inside a loop — you'll hit the 100-query limit fast. Instead, filter with WHERE Id IN :someSet to fetch everything in one query. Second, prefer selective filters on indexed fields so queries stay fast on large data volumes. The binding syntax :variable safely injects Apex variables, including collections, into the query.

SOSL shines when you need to search text across objects — for example finding "Acme" in Accounts, Contacts, and Leads simultaneously with FIND 'Acme*' IN NAME FIELDS RETURNING Account(Name), Contact(LastName). Use SOQL when you know the object and want precise, filtered records; use SOSL when you're searching unstructured text broadly. Next we'll take these query results and modify data with DML.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

posts.title: Learn Salesforce CRM Analytics
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Analytics apps on the Salesforce platform

CRM Analytics (formerly Tableau CRM and Wave) is Salesforce's native analytics engine. It ingests data from Salesforce objects and external systems, stores it in fast columnar datasets, and lets you explore and visualise it in interactive dashboards embedded right inside the CRM. This course gives you the practical workflow used to ship real analytics apps.

We start with the platform overview and setup, then connect data and build datasets. You'll learn the crucial difference between Recipes and Dataflows and when to use each, explore data with Lenses, and assemble dashboards that decision-makers actually use. Two deeper lessons cover SAQL — the query language underneath every widget — and bindings, which make dashboards interactive and dynamic.

Who it's for: admins, analysts, and consultants who want to move beyond standard reports and dashboards. Prerequisites: familiarity with Salesforce objects and reporting. Outcome: you'll be able to prepare data, build a multi-widget dashboard, write SAQL to shape results, and wire up interactivity with bindings. This is a members-only course with a free preview lesson.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Build analytics apps in CRM Analytics (Tableau CRM): datasets, recipes & dataflows, lenses, dashboards, SAQL, and bindings.

posts.title: CRM Analytics Overview & Setup
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

CRM Analytics overview & setup

CRM Analytics — previously Tableau CRM and originally Wave — is Salesforce's native analytics platform. Unlike standard reports and dashboards, which query live Salesforce data directly, CRM Analytics ingests data into its own fast, columnar store called a dataset. This lets it blend Salesforce and external data, handle far larger volumes, and deliver highly interactive, drillable dashboards embedded right inside the CRM.

It helps to know the main building blocks up front. Datasets are the optimised data your analytics run on. Recipes and Dataflows are the two tools that prepare and load data into datasets. Lenses are ad-hoc explorations of a dataset. Dashboards assemble widgets — charts, tables, filters — into an interactive app. Underneath, SAQL (Salesforce Analytics Query Language) is the query language every widget ultimately runs, and bindings make widgets react to each other.

Setup starts with enabling the feature. In Setup, find Analytics (or CRM Analytics) settings and turn it on; your org needs the appropriate licences and permission set licences. Assign users the CRM Analytics Plus or equivalent permission sets — typically a manage/admin set for builders and a view set for consumers. Once enabled, an Analytics Studio app appears in the App Launcher; that's your home base for building datasets, lenses, and dashboards.

A couple of orientation tips. Data security in CRM Analytics is separate from record-level Salesforce sharing — by default a dataset ignores sharing rules unless you apply security predicates, so plan that early for anything sensitive. Also, datasets are a snapshot refreshed on a schedule, not live, so you trade real-time accuracy for speed and scale. With the platform enabled and studio open, the next lesson connects real data and builds your first dataset.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: What CRM Analytics is, how its pieces fit together, and enabling and setting it up in your org.

posts.title: Connecting Data & Building Datasets
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Connecting data & building datasets

Every analysis in CRM Analytics runs on a dataset, so building one is the first practical step. A dataset is a specially indexed copy of your data, tuned for the fast aggregation and filtering that interactive dashboards demand. You create datasets by pulling data in through connectors and shaping it, then registering the result.

The most common source is Salesforce itself. The built-in local Salesforce connector lets you select objects like Opportunity, Account, and User and pull specified fields on a schedule. For data outside Salesforce, external connectors handle sources such as Snowflake, Amazon S3, databases via JDBC, and CSV uploads. Connections sync on a cadence you define — hourly, daily, and so on — landing raw data that your recipes or dataflows then transform.

When you build a dataset, three choices shape its usefulness. First, field selection: pull only the fields you'll analyse, because narrower datasets are faster and cheaper. Second, field types: CRM Analytics classifies every field as a dimension (text you group and filter by), a measure (numbers you aggregate), or a date; getting these right is essential for charts to behave. Third, joins and augmentation: you'll often combine objects — for example augmenting Opportunities with Account and Owner attributes — so a single dataset answers richer questions without runtime joins.

For a first build, use the Salesforce connector to sync Opportunities with a handful of fields (Amount, StageName, CloseDate, AccountId, OwnerId), augment in the Account Industry and Owner Name, and register it as a dataset called "Opportunities". You now have a clean, fast foundation. How you do that shaping — with a Recipe or a Dataflow — is an important design choice, and it's exactly what the next lesson compares.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Connect Salesforce and external data, then create your first optimised dataset for analysis.

posts.title: Recipes vs Dataflows
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Recipes vs Dataflows

CRM Analytics gives you two tools to transform raw connected data into polished datasets: Dataflows and Recipes. They overlap heavily, and knowing when to use each saves a lot of rework. Both read source data, apply transformations, and output one or more registered datasets, but they differ in interface, capability, and direction of travel.

Dataflows are the original tool. You build a JSON-defined pipeline of nodes — sfdcDigest to pull an object, augment to join a related object, computeExpression to derive fields, filter, and sfdcRegister to output the dataset. Dataflows are powerful and well understood, but the editor is more technical and the transformation set is comparatively limited. They run on a schedule and are still common in mature orgs.

Recipes are the modern, recommended tool, built on a more scalable engine. The Recipe editor is visual and interactive: you add input nodes, then transform nodes for join, aggregate, append, filter, transform (cleanse, format, compute columns), and even predict with Einstein Discovery models, previewing sample data at every step. Recipes support far richer transformations, clustering, and multiple outputs, and they generally perform better on large data.

The practical guidance is straightforward: use Recipes for all new development. They're more capable, easier to build and debug thanks to live preview, and are where Salesforce is investing. Keep Dataflows in mind because you'll encounter them in existing orgs and may need to maintain or migrate them, but reach for a Recipe by default. With prepared datasets in hand, the next lesson starts turning them into insight through Lenses.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Compare Recipes and Dataflows for data preparation and learn which to choose for new work.

posts.title: Exploring with Lenses
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Exploring with Lenses

A Lens is an interactive exploration of a single dataset. Think of it as a live question-and-answer session with your data: you pick a measure, group by one or more dimensions, filter, and instantly see the result as a chart or table. Lenses are where analysis actually happens, and every dashboard widget is essentially a saved lens under the hood.

You open a lens by clicking a dataset in Analytics Studio, which drops you into the Explorer. Start by choosing what to measure — Count of Rows by default, or an aggregate like Sum of Amount. Then group by a dimension such as Stage or Industry to break the number down; add a second grouping to create a stacked or grouped breakdown. Apply filters to focus on, say, this quarter's opportunities. The visualisation updates in real time, and you can switch chart types — bar, line, donut, scatter, pivot table — to find the clearest view.

Explorer has two modes worth knowing. The default point-and-click mode is fast for most questions. Toggle to the SAQL editor and you see the underlying query, which is a great way to learn SAQL and to express things the UI can't. Anything you build in a lens can be clipped straight to a dashboard, so exploration flows naturally into dashboard building.

A productive workflow: explore freely in a lens to understand the shape of your data and validate that measures and groupings behave as expected, then save the useful views. Try grouping opportunity Amount by Stage, filtering to the current fiscal year, and flipping between a bar chart and a pivot table. Once you know which views tell the story, you assemble them into a coherent screen — which is the subject of the next lesson on dashboards.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Use Lenses to explore datasets interactively — grouping, measures, filters, and charts — before building dashboards.

posts.title: Building Dashboards
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Building dashboards

A dashboard is the deliverable people actually consume — a single screen of coordinated widgets that answers a business question at a glance and lets viewers drill in. You build dashboards in the CRM Analytics Dashboard Designer, dragging widgets onto a grid and binding each to a query over your datasets.

Widgets come in several kinds. Chart widgets visualise a query as bars, lines, donuts, gauges, and more. Table widgets show values or compare records. Number widgets highlight a single KPI. Filter, list, date, and toggle widgets let users slice the data. Text, image, and container widgets handle layout and branding. Each data widget runs its own query, which you can build with clicks or in SAQL.

The feature that makes CRM Analytics dashboards feel alive is faceting. When widgets share the same dataset, selecting a value in one automatically filters the others — click a bar for "Technology" and every other widget narrows to Technology, with no configuration required. For cross-dataset or conditional interactivity you use explicit bindings, covered in a later lesson. Global filters and a filter panel give users controlled ways to change scope.

Design for the audience. Lead with the headline KPI, arrange supporting charts in a logical reading order, keep the widget count restrained, and use the responsive layout options so it works on the devices people actually use, including the Salesforce mobile app. Build a real one: a Number widget for total pipeline, a bar chart of Amount by Stage, a donut of Amount by Industry, and a filter for fiscal quarter — all faceting together. That is a genuinely useful sales dashboard. To push interactivity further and to shape queries precisely, the next lessons cover SAQL and bindings.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

posts.title: What CPQ Solves & the Conga Landscape
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

What CPQ solves & the Conga landscape

CPQ stands for Configure, Price, Quote, and it exists to fix a painful, revenue-critical problem: turning a complex product catalog into a fast, accurate, approved quote. Without CPQ, sales reps build quotes in spreadsheets, mis-configure bundles, apply the wrong discounts, and route approvals by email. The result is slow deals, pricing errors, and revenue leakage. CPQ automates configuration rules, pricing logic, and approval workflows so reps produce correct quotes in minutes.

The three letters map to three jobs. Configure ensures the products and options a rep selects are valid combinations — you can't sell a licence without its required platform, and incompatible add-ons are blocked. Price applies the right list prices, volume tiers, discounts, and currency conversions consistently. Quote assembles the priced configuration into a professional, approved document the customer can sign. CPQ sits in the middle of the broader quote-to-cash process, downstream of opportunity management and upstream of contracts, billing, and revenue.

Conga CPQ — formerly Apttus CPQ — is a native Salesforce application, meaning it runs inside your org on the platform rather than as a separate system. It's part of the wider Conga suite, which also includes CLM (Contract Lifecycle Management), Conga Composer and Conga Sign for document generation and e-signature, and Billing. In practice CPQ often connects to CLM for contracts and to Composer for polished quote documents, forming an end-to-end revenue platform.

Why this matters for you: CPQ is one of the highest-value, best-paid Salesforce specialisms precisely because it sits on revenue and is genuinely complex. This course focuses on the big-picture architecture — how catalog, pricing, rules, approvals, and documents connect — so you understand the system rather than memorising screens that change between releases. With the landscape mapped, the next lesson dives into the foundation everything rests on: the product catalog and bundles.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Why CPQ exists, the problems it solves on the quote-to-cash path, and where Conga CPQ sits in the product landscape.

posts.title: Product Catalog & Bundles
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Product catalog & bundles

Everything in CPQ starts with the product catalog — the structured library of what your company sells. In Conga CPQ the catalog is built on Salesforce's Product2 object extended with CPQ-specific fields and related configuration. Getting the catalog model right is the single most important design task in an implementation, because pricing, rules, and quoting all depend on it.

Products come in a few shapes. A standalone product is a simple sellable item with a price. A bundle is a parent product that contains other products as options, organised into option groups. For example a "Platform Suite" bundle might have an option group "Core" with a required platform licence, and an option group "Add-ons" with optional modules. Option groups control cardinality — minimum and maximum selections — so you can require exactly one platform but allow several add-ons.

Several modelling concepts give bundles their power. Product options define how a child sits inside a bundle: default quantity, whether it's required, and whether its quantity is editable. Attributes capture configurable characteristics — colour, tier, term length — that can drive both pricing and rules. Nested bundles let a bundle contain other bundles for deep product hierarchies. Well-designed attributes and option groups mean the configuration UI guides reps to valid selections naturally.

A practical modelling mindset: start from how the business actually sells, not from the objects. Identify the true bundles, the required versus optional components, the sensible defaults, and the attributes that vary a product. Keep the hierarchy as shallow as the business allows, because deep nesting complicates pricing and performance. A clean catalog makes the next topics — pricing, then constraint rules — dramatically simpler, which is exactly where we go next.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Model products in Conga CPQ: the catalog, standalone products, option groups, bundles, and configuration attributes.

posts.title: Pricing: Lists, Tiers & Matrices
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Pricing: lists, tiers & matrices

Once products are configured, CPQ must price them, and Conga's pricing engine is both flexible and layered. At the foundation is the price list: a named collection of price list items (PLIs), each linking a product to a price in a currency. A quote is associated with a price list, and the engine looks up each line's PLI to find its base price. Companies commonly maintain multiple price lists for different regions, segments, or partner tiers.

Base prices are rarely the whole story, so CPQ layers pricing methods on top. Tiered pricing changes the price based on quantity or amount — for example a lower unit price above 100 seats — and can be applied as a block (all units at the tier price) or as a graduated slab (each tier priced separately). Price matrices (also called price dimensions or matrix pricing) look up a price or adjustment from a table keyed by one or more dimensions such as term length, region, and attribute values, letting you express complex rate cards declaratively.

On top of base and tier pricing sit adjustments. These include discounts and markups applied at the line or summary level, as absolute amounts or percentages, manually by the rep or automatically by rules. CPQ also handles proration for partial terms, currency conversion, and the distinction between one-time and recurring charges — critical for subscription businesses where a line has an annual or monthly cadence.

The engine applies these in a defined price waterfall: base price, then tier or matrix adjustments, then rule-driven and manual adjustments, arriving at a net price the customer sees. Understanding that waterfall is key to troubleshooting "why is this line priced like that?" — you trace each step. Pricing and configuration together produce a valid, correctly priced quote, but keeping configurations valid at scale needs rules, which the next lesson covers.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

posts.title: Constraint Rules & Guided Selling
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Constraint rules & guided selling

A rich catalog can be configured in invalid ways, so CPQ uses constraint rules to enforce what combinations are allowed and to help reps sell correctly. Constraint rules run during configuration and react to what the rep has selected, either blocking invalid choices or automatically adjusting the cart. They are what stop a quote from containing a module without its prerequisite, or two mutually exclusive options together.

Conga constraint rules come in recognisable types. An inclusion rule says "if product A is selected, product B must also be included" — useful for required prerequisites, and it can auto-add B. An exclusion rule says "if A is selected, B cannot be", preventing incompatible combinations. A validation rule checks a condition and shows an error or warning without necessarily changing the cart — for example flagging that a discount exceeds policy. A recommendation rule suggests complementary products to drive cross-sell. Each rule has a condition (what triggers it) and an action (what it enforces).

Guided selling approaches the problem from the front end. Instead of dropping a rep into a large catalog, guided selling asks a few business questions — company size, industry, use case — and uses the answers to pre-filter or pre-configure the right products. It shortens ramp time for new reps and steers deals toward validated, profitable configurations. Technically it's often implemented with a search or questionnaire that maps answers to product selections and applicable rules.

Designing rules well is a balance. Too few and reps build broken quotes; too many or poorly scoped and configuration becomes slow and frustrating, and performance suffers because every rule evaluates on each change. Aim for the minimum set of clear rules that enforce genuine business constraints, name them meaningfully, and test them against real selling scenarios. Valid, well-guided configurations then flow into the approval and discounting controls we cover next.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Keep configurations valid and guide reps with constraint rules — inclusion, exclusion, validation — and guided selling flows.

posts.title: Approvals & Deal Guidance
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Approvals & deal guidance

Once a rep can configure and price a quote, the business needs guardrails so discounts and terms stay within policy. Conga CPQ provides an approvals framework and deal guidance that together govern how much freedom reps have and when a deal needs sign-off. This is where finance and sales leadership encode their rules into the quoting process.

Approval processes are triggered by conditions on the quote — a discount above a threshold, a non-standard term, a price below floor, or a large deal size. When triggered, the quote routes to one or more approvers, often in a matrix that escalates by severity: a small extra discount goes to a sales manager, a deep one to the VP or finance. Approvals can be sequential or parallel, support delegation and recall, and block the quote from being finalised until cleared. The rep sees the pending approvals and their status directly on the quote.

Deal guidance (and related deal maximizer concepts) helps reps price well before they hit an approval wall. It surfaces target, floor, and stretch pricing, shows how a proposed discount compares to policy or to similar historical deals, and nudges reps toward the best acceptable price. Where approvals are a control, guidance is coaching — reducing the number of quotes that need escalation in the first place by helping reps get it right.

Designing this layer is about balancing speed and control. Set thresholds that catch genuinely risky deals without forcing approval on routine ones, keep approval chains short enough to avoid bottlenecks, and give clear reasons and guidance so reps understand why a deal needs sign-off. Well-tuned approvals plus proactive guidance protect margin while keeping the sales cycle fast. With a valid, priced, and approved quote in hand, the final step is producing the customer-facing document, which the last lesson covers.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
posts.custom_excerpt: Control discounting and risk with approval processes and deal guidance so quotes stay within policy.

posts.title: Quotes, Renewals & Document Generation
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Quotes, renewals & document generation

The end product of CPQ is a quote — the finalised, priced, approved offer — and the customer-facing document that presents it. In Conga CPQ the quote is a record (the Proposal / Quote object) that carries the configured line items, totals, terms, and approval status. From it you generate a polished proposal, send it for signature, and, once won, feed it into contracts and billing.

Document generation is typically handled by Conga Composer and templates. Composer merges quote data into professionally formatted Word, PDF, or PowerPoint templates, so the customer receives a branded proposal with the right line items, pricing, terms, and legal language — no manual assembly. Paired with Conga Sign or another e-signature tool, the proposal goes out, gets signed, and returns, all tracked against the quote. This automation eliminates the copy-paste errors that plague spreadsheet quoting.

Subscription and enterprise businesses depend heavily on two lifecycle operations. A renewal creates a new quote from an existing contract as its term ends, carrying forward products and pricing with any uplift, so recurring revenue is captured without rebuilding the deal. An amendment (or change order) modifies an in-flight contract mid-term — adding seats, upgrading tiers, or co-terminating add-ons — with CPQ handling proration so the customer is billed correctly for the partial period. These flows connect CPQ to CLM and billing, closing the quote-to-cash loop.

Stepping back, you've now seen the whole picture: the catalog and bundles model what you sell, pricing computes the numbers, constraint rules and guided selling keep configurations valid, approvals and deal guidance protect margin, and quotes, renewals, amendments, and document generation deliver and sustain the deal. That end-to-end mental model is exactly what makes a strong CPQ consultant — you can now reason about any part of an implementation and how it connects to the rest.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

LWC intro & course trailer

Welcome to Lightning Web Components A–Z. Lightning Web Components (LWC) is Salesforce's modern UI framework, and unlike its predecessor Aura it's built directly on web standards: native custom elements, shadow DOM, ES modules, and plain modern JavaScript. That means the skills you build here are largely transferable web-development skills, with a thin Salesforce-specific layer on top. If you know ES6, you already know most of LWC.

Why did Salesforce build LWC? Performance and standards. Because it leans on what the browser provides natively rather than a heavy framework layer, LWC renders faster and has a smaller footprint than Aura. It coexists with Aura — the two can even interoperate — but LWC is the future and where all new investment goes. For anyone building on the platform today, it's the default choice for custom UI.

Across this course you'll go from an empty component to a tested, deployed feature. We'll dissect a component's anatomy — its HTML template, JavaScript class, and metadata file — then cover reactivity, template directives, and getters. You'll learn to handle events and let components communicate, wire real Salesforce data with Apex and Lightning Data Service, and use platform services for navigation, toasts, and error handling. The final lessons cover unit testing with Jest and deploying to an org with the Salesforce CLI.

This first lesson is a trailer, so there's no setup required yet — just orientation. To follow along in later lessons you'll want a Salesforce org and the Salesforce CLI with a code editor like VS Code and the Salesforce Extension Pack, which we'll set up when we deploy. posts.title: Deploying to an Org
posts.lexical:
{"root":{"children":[{"type":"html","version":1,"html":"

Deploying to an org

A component isn't useful until it's in an org, and the modern way to get it there is the Salesforce CLI (sf) working against a source-format project. You develop locally in VS Code with the Salesforce Extension Pack, keep your metadata in version control, and deploy to orgs on demand. There are two common workflows: scratch orgs with source tracking for development, and direct metadata deploys to persistent orgs like sandboxes and production.

First you authorise an org so the CLI can talk to it, then deploy your source. During development against a scratch or tracked org you can push and pull changes; against a sandbox or production you deploy a specified set of metadata.

# Authorise a sandbox or production org (opens a browser login)
sf org login web --alias myorg --instance-url https://test.salesforce.com

# Deploy the LWC (and related metadata) to that org
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app/main/default/lwc --target-org myorg

# For scratch-org development with source tracking:
sf project deploy start --target-org scratchOrg   # push local changes
sf project retrieve start --target-org scratchOrg # pull org changes

# Run local Jest tests before deploying
npm run test:unit

# Run Apex tests in the org after deploy
sf apex run test --target-org myorg --wait 10 --result-format human

A few practices keep deployments smooth. Deploy the whole feature, not just the component: an LWC often depends on Apex classes, custom fields, and permission sets, so include them or the deploy fails. Validate before you commit to production with a check-only deploy (--dry-run) and run the required Apex tests, since production deploys must meet the 75% coverage rule. Use source tracking in scratch orgs and sandboxes so the CLI knows exactly what changed, avoiding accidental overwrites.

For team delivery, wire these commands into a CI/CD pipeline so every change is validated and deployed automatically, and manage promotion from sandbox to production through version control rather than manual clicks. That completes the LWC journey: you can now build a component, make it reactive, wire in real data, add navigation and feedback, test it with Jest, and deploy it to any org. From here, keep building — the best way to cement all of this is to ship a small component of your own into a Developer org today.

"}],"direction":"ltr","format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
